## About This Talk {.heading-accent}

- What you're about to hear is one just person's opinion.
- "Prediction is hard, especially about the future." Take predictions with a
  grain of salt.
  - We will all work up to 40 years, and some of us will live 80 more, in the
    long-term horizon all bets are off.
- Nothing here is Excella policy or an Excella recommendation
- This talk was built with AI assistance
  - Fact checking was done by me and errors are my own
- Universal advice, especially important in the AI age back up your data, and manage risk appropriately

::: {.notes}
Audience context (don't necessarily show this table, but calibrate
depth to it): 72 unique confirmed attendees, cross-referenced against LinkedIn
role data. ~54% of the full list are identifiable technical practitioners (75%
of the 52 people we could classify at all); the rest split between people
management/BA/delivery roles and unknowns. Pitch explanations so a non-coder in
the room isn't lost, but don't undersell the technical crowd.
:::

## If You Take Away Anything From This Talk {background-color="#0d4a55" .stat-slide}

AI progress, job/task replacement, and "the future" all come back to one
question:

::: {.r-fit-text}

> Can you find a fast, cheap, trustworthy way to check an answer?

:::

Everything else in this talk is downstream of that.

# Part 1: The Magic {background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #073642 55%, #0f4d4d 100%)" .divider-slide}

<!-- STAGE 1/9 (llm-stage-1-language): language: small constituency tree, "king" glides on to stage 2 -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-1-language auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="language"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li><strong>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This is the raw material every LLM starts from: human language is dense
(a huge amount of meaning per token) and context-sensitive (the same word
means different things depending on what's around it). The tree shown is
a standard constituency parse -- the kind of structure a formal,
context-free grammar can assign to a sentence, same idea as parsing a
programming language.

Worth saying out loud, not shown on the slide: natural language actually
exceeds that. Per the Chomsky hierarchy (regular &sub; context-free &sub;
context-sensitive &sub; recursively enumerable), natural language is not
regular and not context-free, and arguably isn't fully captured by any
formal grammar at all -- unlike programming languages, which are
deliberately designed to stay context-free so they can be parsed
efficiently. This tree is a simplification for the sake of legibility,
not a claim that this fully describes what's really going on.

That gap is also where LLMs' real weakness shows up: DeepMind's "Neural
Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy" (Del&eacute;tang et al., ICLR 2023,
arXiv:2207.02098) tests transformers against tasks at each hierarchy
level and finds they reliably fail to generalize on tasks needing
unbounded exact recursion or counting (e.g. matching parentheses nested
deeper than anything seen in training) -- self-attention has no built-in
stack. Ironically, transformers can be worse at some simple, formally
regular languages than they are at messy natural language, because
natural language is statistically forgiving in a way strict formal
languages aren't.

Nobody engineered context-sensitivity into the model; it's a property of
the input the model has to somehow represent -- which is exactly what
embeddings are for, next slide.
:::

<!-- STAGE 2/9 (llm-stage-2-embeddings): embeddings: 3 orthogonal axes + 1 point -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-2-embeddings auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="embeddings"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li><strong>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Every word/token gets mapped to a point (a vector) in a numerical space
&mdash; that's the entire trick that lets a neural network do math on
language at all. This axis diagram is a toy 3-dimensional stand-in;
real embedding spaces have hundreds to thousands of dimensions.
:::

<!-- STAGE 3/9 (llm-stage-3-vector-math): vector math: king-man+woman=queen, two parallel analogy pairs -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-3-vector-math auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="vector-math"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li><strong>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The classic demonstration: king &minus; man + woman &approx; queen, shown
here as an actual walked vector path (king, then subtract man's vector,
then add woman's vector, landing on queen) rather than just an implied
relationship between unlabeled points &mdash; the offset from man to woman
and the offset from king to queen are the same vector, meaning the space
has learned a consistent "gender" direction without ever being told one
exists. Classic reference: Mikolov et al., "Linguistic Regularities in
Continuous Space Word Representations" (NAACL 2013) and the original
word2vec paper (Mikolov et al. 2013, arXiv:1301.3781). Worth saying out
loud: this is a genuinely simplified, best-case illustration &mdash; real
analogy performance is noisier and more brittle than the clean textbook
examples, and modern LLM embeddings are far higher-
dimensional and contextual (not one fixed vector per word) than this toy
picture shows.
:::

<!-- STAGE 4/9 (llm-stage-4-latent-space): latent space: 4 verified near-orthogonal words fade in around king -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-4-latent-space auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="latent-space"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li><strong>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The math: in d exactly-orthogonal dimensions, you can only fit d mutually
orthogonal directions &mdash; but exponentially many nearly-orthogonal
directions exist in the same space (the intuition behind the
Johnson&ndash;Lindenstrauss lemma). Anthropic's "Toy Models of Superposition"
(2022, transformer-circuits.pub) shows real neural networks exploit exactly
this: they represent far more features/concepts than they have literal
dimensions by encoding them as almost-orthogonal directions, tolerating a
small amount of cross-feature interference &mdash; especially cheap when
features are sparse (rarely active at once). Without relaxed orthogonality,
a model would be limited to roughly as many independent concepts as it has
dimensions; real embedding spaces pack in vastly more than that (Anthropic's
"Scaling Monosemanticity" work found millions of interpretable feature
directions in a model with only a few thousand dimensions &mdash; direct
evidence this isn't just theoretical). The four words shown here
(drill/supernova/photosynthesis/asteroid) aren't picked for vibes &mdash;
checked against real glove-wiki-gigaword-100 embeddings, their cosine
similarity with "king" is 0.011/0.016/-0.004/-0.019 respectively, genuinely
within a hair of zero. A tempting fourth candidate ("whiteboard") looked
just as intuitively unrelated but actually came back at -0.28 &mdash; a
real example of why it's worth checking instead of assuming.
:::

<!-- STAGE 5/9 (llm-stage-5-transformer): transformer: unlabeled sketch, king glides in as the input -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-5-transformer auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="transformer"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</li>
      <li><strong>A highly parameterized statistical model (the Transformer)</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>Kimi K3 totals (2.8T total, 104B activated per token): Kimi Team (Moonshot AI), <a href="https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3" target="_blank" rel="noopener">model card</a> and <a href="https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3/blob/main/k3_tech_report.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">technical report</a> -- current largest open-weight model, released July 2026, surpassing Kimi K2 (1T, used on this slide previously) and DeepSeek V4 Pro (1.6T)</li>
        <li>No attention/feed-forward breakdown is shown for K3 (unlike the earlier K2 version of this slide) -- K3 uses a hybrid attention mechanism, mostly a linear "Kimi Delta Attention" plus some full-attention layers, and there's no verified parameter-counting formula on hand for that mechanism the way there was for K2's MLA (cross-checked against DeepSeek-V3's own published figures)</li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
In statistical-learning terms: "highly parameterized" means a very large
number of free/trainable weights, giving the model enough capacity
(degrees of freedom) to approximate a highly complex, non-linear,
high-dimensional function without underfitting. Neural networks are
universal function approximators in the limit (Universal Approximation
Theorem) &mdash; the practical question is always whether a given
architecture/parameter-count/data combination gets close enough. The
Transformer's specific contribution is multi-head self-attention: every
token can directly attend to every other token in context, capturing
long-range dependencies that lower-capacity models (n-grams, bag-of-words,
fixed-window models) structurally cannot represent.

The sketch shown here is deliberately unlabeled -- same silhouette as the
real decoder-only Transformer diagram in "The Transformer Still Rules"
(embedding at the bottom, a repeated norm/attention/residual/norm/FFN/
residual block, final norm, then linear+softmax at the top) but shaded
out and stripped of every label, since none of that detail has been
introduced yet. "king" is shown gliding in as the input token feeding
the bottom of the stack -- the full labeled version comes later.

Small note beside the sketch (drawn right in the panel, not a table
anymore): "2.8 trillion parameters -- Kimi K3, approx." Kimi K3
(Moonshot AI) is the current largest open-weight model, released July
2026 -- it superseded an earlier version of this slide that used Kimi
K2 (1T) with a full attention-vs-feed-forward breakdown. That breakdown
isn't shown for K3: K3's attention is a hybrid mechanism (mostly a
linear "Kimi Delta Attention," with some full-attention layers mixed
in), and there's no verified parameter-counting formula on hand for it
the way there was for K2's MLA. Rather than publish an unverified split,
this slide only shows the one number Kimi K3 itself publishes with
confidence (2.8T total, 104B activated per token -- see Sources).

Worth saying out loud instead, as a general rule rather than a
K3-specific figure: across transformer architectures, feed-forward
layers hold noticeably more parameters than attention, and the gap is
much bigger for Mixture-of-Experts models like this one than for dense
ones. In a plain dense transformer (no MoE), standard attention (Q/K/V/O
projections) and a standard 4x-expansion feed-forward block work out to
roughly a 1:2 ratio -- feed-forward is about two-thirds of the
attention+feed-forward total, attention about a third. MoE skews that
much further toward feed-forward, since the model multiplies out many
parallel expert feed-forward blocks while attention stays roughly
constant per layer -- on Kimi K2 specifically (verified from its
published config, not estimated), feed-forward was over 99% of
attention+feed-forward combined. K3 is an even larger MoE (896 experts
vs K2's 384), so if asked "roughly how much is feed-forward," "the
large majority -- often 90%+, sometimes higher still for very sparse
MoE designs" is a defensible generalization even without a verified K3-
specific number. The remainder, wherever it lives across these
architectures, is mostly token embeddings and the output/vocabulary
projection, plus a genuinely negligible amount in normalization layers
-- not attention and not feed-forward.
:::

<!-- STAGE 6/9 (llm-stage-6-data): data: Common Crawl vs. used-after-filtering bars -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-6-data auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="data"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</li>
      <li>A highly parameterized statistical model (the Transformer)</li>
      <li><strong>Lots of data</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>Common Crawl token estimate (~240T): <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02595" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Nemotron-CC</a> (arXiv:2412.02595), <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557" target="_blank" rel="noopener">FineWeb</a> (arXiv:2406.17557, NeurIPS 2024)</li>
        <li>GPT-3's ~82% Common Crawl share (Table 2.2): <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Language Models are Few-Shot Learners"</a> (arXiv:2005.14165)</li>
        <li>64% of 47 surveyed LLMs trained on Common Crawl: Mozilla Foundation, <a href="https://www.mozillafoundation.org/en/research/library/generative-ai-training-data/common-crawl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Training Data for the Price of a Sandwich"</a> (2024)</li>
        <li>Total stock (~300T) &amp; ~2028 wall: Villalobos et al., <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.04325" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data"</a>, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2211.04325)</li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
<template id="llm-axes-source-data">
{{< include images/llm-ingredients-data-volume.svg >}}
</template>
```

::: {.notes}
Common Crawl (all pre-2023 snapshots) is estimated at roughly 240 trillion
tokens. Frontier models pretrain on roughly 10&ndash;20 trillion tokens
after heavy quality filtering &mdash; a small fraction of raw Common Crawl.
GPT-3 drew ~82% of its raw training tokens from Common Crawl; a 2023 survey
found at least 64% of 47 published LLMs used it. Caveat to say out loud:
"% of the internet" is a genuinely fuzzy, often-inflated claim in popular
discourse &mdash; Common Crawl is a large but incomplete, English-skewed,
spam-heavy crawl of the public web, not literally "the internet."

The third bar (~300T, "the wall"): Villalobos et al., "Will We Run Out of
Data?" (arXiv:2211.04325; the ~300T figure and 2026&ndash;2032 exhaustion
window are from the 2024 ICML revision, not the original 2022 arXiv draft
&mdash; worth knowing since the two versions disagree by ~30x and it's easy
to accidentally cite the stale one). 90% CI: 100T&ndash;1000T &mdash; say
the range out loud, this is a highly uncertain estimate, not a precise
count.

Exactly how 300T relates to Common Crawl's 240T, if asked (this came up
live and is worth having cold): the paper tracks TWO separate stock
estimates, not one. "Low-quality" general web text (all of it, including
Reddit, forums, social media, everything beyond any single crawl) they put
at ~741 trillion words, with a genuinely huge uncertainty band (68T to
71,000T) &mdash; so yes, there is more raw text out there than Common Crawl
alone, that intuition is correct. But the ~300T "effective stock" headline
number is NOT derived from that 741T low-quality pool. It's built from
their much smaller "high-quality" branch (books + papers + code + curated
web, originally ~9T words in 2022), scaled up 5x after they found that
carefully-filtered web text performs as well as curated corpora, then
another 2&ndash;5x from multi-epoch training (reusing the same tokens
across multiple passes). So "300T" measures usable, quality-filtered,
practically-trainable text, not literally everything that exists &mdash;
a much bigger low-quality pool exists but doesn't meaningfully extend the
wall, since redundant/spammy text doesn't add much training value. Books
specifically, since it's a natural follow-up: the paper's own estimate for
the ENTIRE stock of books ever published is only 620 billion to 1.8
trillion words (10&ndash;30 million ebooks) &mdash; real, and legally
significant (Books3, LibGen, Anthropic's 2025 author settlement), but small
next to web-scale numbers. One honest gap: the paper only counts publicly
scrapable text; proprietary licensing deals (Reddit-Google, News Corp-
OpenAI, etc.) aren't separately quantified, so labs' actual usable pool
could run somewhat higher, though those deals are mostly about access
rights to platforms already reflected in the low-quality estimate, not
undiscovered volume.

At current dataset-size growth trends (each model generation using more
data than the last), the paper's headline result is that training sets
converge on the size of the entire effective stock between 2026 and 2032
(80% CI), median ~2028 at compute-optimal training &mdash; faster
(2025&ndash;2027) if labs lean into overtraining smaller models on more
tokens, which is exactly the current industry trend. Beyond that, further
scaling leans on synthetic data, multimodal data (video/audio/images),
code, and squeezing more epochs out of existing text.
:::

<!-- STAGE 7/9 (llm-stage-7-compute): compute: FLOPs-over-time bars -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-7-compute auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="compute"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</li>
      <li>A highly parameterized statistical model (the Transformer)</li>
      <li>Lots of data</li>
      <li><strong>Lots of compute to train</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>2019 baseline &amp; 2026 frontier estimate (1e26&ndash;1e27 FLOPs): <a href="https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/research-and-development" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Stanford HAI AI Index 2025</a>, Research and Development chapter</li>
        <li>GPT-4 (~2e25 FLOPs) and other models trained at GPT-4 scale: Epoch AI, <a href="https://epoch.ai/data-insights/models-over-1e25-flop" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Over 30 AI models have been trained at the scale of GPT-4"</a></li>
        <li>Training cost figures (GPT-4 ~$78&ndash;80M, Llama 3.1 405B ~$170M): Stanford HAI AI Index 2025 / Epoch AI cost estimates</li>
        <li>2030 compute ceiling (~2e29 FLOPs) &amp; power/chip bottleneck: Epoch AI, <a href="https://epoch.ai/publications/can-ai-scaling-continue-through-2030" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030?"</a></li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
<template id="llm-axes-source-compute">
{{< include images/llm-ingredients-compute-scale.svg >}}
</template>
```

::: {.notes}
GPT-4: ~2.1&times;10^25 FLOPs, ~$78&ndash;80M to train (Stanford AI Index /
Epoch AI estimates). Llama 3.1 405B: ~$170M. 2026-era frontier runs:
estimated 1&times;10^26 to 1&times;10^27 FLOPs, $200&ndash;500M, with
projections toward $1&ndash;3B by late 2027. Training compute has scaled
roughly 4&ndash;5x per year historically (note: this is FLOPs growth,
not cost growth -- Epoch AI separately finds training *cost* has grown
a slower 2&ndash;3x/year over the past 8 years, since hardware and
algorithmic efficiency gains absorb some of the compute growth without
a proportional cost increase).

The fourth bar, if asked "is there a limit?": Epoch AI's "Can AI Scaling
Continue Through 2030?" (2024) is the closest thing to a real answer.
Their finding: no hard wall yet, but not unlimited either. Training runs
around ~2x10^29 FLOPs are likely feasible by 2030 -- roughly the same
size jump over today's frontier as GPT-4 was over GPT-2. Power is "the
constraint likely to bind first": frontier training power draw has been
growing ~2.2x/year and already exceeds 100MW; by 2030 the largest runs
could need 4&ndash;16 GW, requiring genuinely new power-plant and grid
buildout, not just more chips. Chip manufacturing capacity (advanced
packaging/HBM production, not raw fab capacity) binds second -- their
median 2030 estimate is ~100 million H100-equivalent GPUs dedicated to
training. Data and network-latency constraints matter less than power
or chips under current projections. Bottom line for the room: the
economic/energy wall is real but a few years out, not something we're
already up against the way the data wall increasingly is.
:::

<!-- STAGE 8/9 (llm-stage-8-training): training: shared shaded LLM box, now with real FFN/attention-head mini-networks inside it (active teal), plus a training-specific worked example: "The king wore a [blank]" with a data-size caption and input arrow -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-8-training auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="training"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</li>
      <li>A highly parameterized statistical model (the Transformer)</li>
      <li>Lots of data</li>
      <li>Lots of compute to train</li>
      <li><strong>A training process</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>405B parameters: Grattafiori et al. (Meta), <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"The Llama 3 Herd of Models"</a> (arXiv:2407.21783) -- same model already cited on the compute slide's "Llama 3.1 405B: ~$170M" bar</li>
        <li>~15&ndash;20T tokens: same post-filtering figure as the data slide's "used after filtering" bar -- see that slide's sources (Villalobos et al., arXiv:2211.04325)</li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The loop: run the model forward on a batch, compare its prediction to the
real next token (the loss), compute gradients backward through every
parameter, nudge every weight slightly to reduce that loss, repeat &mdash;
millions to billions of times, over weeks. This is what stages 6 and 7
(data and compute) actually get spent on.

Diagram: the same shaded box from stage 5, but its attention and
feed-forward regions are no longer plain shaded rectangles -- they now
show small illustrative dots-and-lines networks standing in for the
model's actual parameters, drawn active/teal this stage to signal
they're all being adjusted this pass. FFN is 3 columns (2 in, 3
hidden/expanded, 2 out) -- 2 layers of connections, matching the real
FFN's up-project-then-down-project shape. Attention is three small
parallel clusters, a simplified stand-in for multiple heads operating
in parallel rather than one pooled network. Up top, past the grey
output arrow (the same slot "Charles III" occupies on the other two
stages), sits what training actually optimizes for: not the "who is
the king" question from stage 5, but the exact stage-1 sentence with
its last word masked out -- "The king wore a [blank]" -- since
predicting the missing/next word IS the training objective. Down at
the input, instead of one example sentence, a caption reading "~15-20T
tokens" feeds into the arrow -- the bulk corpus (same post-filter
figure as stage 6), not a single instance. Same mini-networks reappear
on the next slide (inference) with the lines dimmed and lock icons
beside them instead -- the explicit visual contrast is the point:
training changes every one of those parameters, inference changes none
of them.
:::

<!-- STAGE 9/9 (llm-stage-9-inference): inference: shared shaded LLM box, mini-networks dimmed with a lock icon, reusing stage 5's exact "Who is the current UK king ?" -> "Charles III" worked example instead of a generic token-count figure -->
## The Ingredients of an LLM {#llm-stage-9-inference auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual">
    <div class="llm-axes-anchor" data-axes-stage="inference"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>An informationally dense, context-sensitive language</li>
      <li>A way to turn words into numbers (embeddings)</li>
      <li>A geometry where semantic relationships become vector arithmetic</li>
      <li>A latent space that relaxes orthogonality to pack in more information</li>
      <li>A highly parameterized statistical model (the Transformer)</li>
      <li>Lots of data</li>
      <li>Lots of compute to train</li>
      <li>A training process</li>
      <li><strong>An inference process</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>405B parameters: Grattafiori et al. (Meta), <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"The Llama 3 Herd of Models"</a> (arXiv:2407.21783) -- same model already cited on the compute and training slides</li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Inference is training's read-only sibling: one forward pass through the
already-trained, frozen weights, producing a probability distribution over
the next token, then sampling from it &mdash; no gradients, no weight
updates, no loss computed. Repeat one token at a time to generate a full
response. This is why inference is orders of magnitude cheaper than
training: no backward pass, no millions of repetitions, no updating billions
of parameters each step.

Diagram: same box, same FFN/attention mini-networks as the training
slide, same dots, but the lines are dimmed now and a small padlock icon
sits beside each of the two (one for FFN, one for attention) instead of
glowing active teal -- none of those parameters change during inference,
which is exactly why it's so much
cheaper than training. The input/output side deliberately reuses stage
5's exact worked example (the same "Who is the current UK king ?"
sentence, the same input arrow, the same "Charles III" answer, king
gliding into the same spot) rather than a token-count figure: inference
is one sentence in, one answer out, not a corpus, so the visual should
look like a single pass, not a pile of data. Not yet visualized here but
worth saying out loud if there's time: the KV cache (why generating
token N+1 doesn't redo the work for tokens 1..N) and the actual sampled
next-token result -- candidates for a future pass if there's room.
:::

## The Transformer Still Rules {.heading-accent}

::: {style="text-align: center;"}

```{=html}
{{< include images/decoder-only-transformer.svg >}}
```

:::

::: {.notes}
This is a decoder-only Transformer — the architecture behind GPT, Claude,
Llama, and effectively every mainstream LLM today. The original "Attention Is
All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017) diagram was encoder-decoder, built for
machine translation (encode a source sentence, decode into a target
language). Modern LLMs drop the encoder and its cross-attention entirely,
keeping only the stack of masked self-attention + feed-forward blocks shown
here, repeated N times, generating one token at a time from everything
generated so far. Attention: every token can directly attend to every other
token (up to and including itself, masked so it can't see the future), in
parallel — no recurrence needed. The KV cache is what makes autoregressive
generation tractable: keys/values for already-seen tokens are computed once
and reused, not recomputed every step.

Residual (a.k.a. skip) connections — each "+" in the diagram is `output = x +
Sublayer(x)`: the sublayer's input `x` is carried around it unchanged and
added back to its output. `x` is a per-token activation vector, not a set of
weights — its very first version comes out of Token Embedding + Positional
Encoding at the bottom of the stack, and each block's job is just to update
it. "Skip" names the topology (the connection skips over the block);
"residual" names what the block has to learn — a correction on top of the
input, rather than the full transformation from scratch.
Motivation: this comes from ResNet (2015, image classification), which found
that plain deep networks got _worse_ at training error (not just test error)
as more layers were added — proof it was an optimization problem, not
overfitting. The residual fixes it by giving gradients a direct identity
path back to early layers during backprop, so they don't have to be
multiplied through every layer's Jacobian to get there — that's the
vanishing-gradient mitigation. This is what makes stacking dozens (or 100+)
of Transformer blocks trainable at all. One more detail baked into this
diagram: it's drawn pre-norm (Norm happens before the sublayer, residual
added after) — what GPT-2 onward and Llama use, versus the original 2017
paper's post-norm (normalize after the add). Pre-norm is more stable at
scale, part of why it's now near-universal.

What each piece in the diagram is actually for:

- **Token Embedding + Positional Encoding** — turns discrete tokens into
  continuous vectors the network can do math on, and injects order
  information, since attention itself is permutation-invariant and has no
  built-in sense of sequence order without this.
- **Norm** (before each sublayer, plus once at the end) — keeps activation
  magnitudes stable as values pass through many stacked layers, stopping
  them from exploding or shrinking with depth. A big part of why stacks of
  dozens of blocks are trainable at all, alongside the residuals above.
- **Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention** — lets every token gather information
  from every earlier token (masked so it can't see the future, required for
  autoregressive generation). "Multi-head" runs several attention patterns
  in parallel subspaces, so the model can track different kinds of
  relationships at once (e.g., syntax vs. coreference vs. topic) instead of
  being forced into a single pattern.
  - **Why multiple heads**: we need multiple heads because language is
    complex — there are many distinct aspects of it that need attending to
    at once, and a single head can only capture one such pattern at a time.
  - **Why multiple blocks**: we need multiple blocks because facts and
    features compound — each block adds a new vector directly into the same
    running per-token representation (the residual stream), a literal
    additive update, not a repeated attempt, so a later block can depend on
    something only an earlier block could have produced. In specific traced
    cases we can name exactly what gets added: a "previous-token" signal
    enabling pattern-completion (induction heads), or accumulated facts
    about a specific entity enabling multi-hop recall (factual lookup
    circuits). What a given block adds in the general case isn't known —
    an open problem, not a detail being skipped.
- **KV Cache** — avoids recomputing keys/values for every earlier token at
  every generation step; without it, generating token N would mean
  reprocessing the entire prefix from scratch each time.
- **Feed-Forward Network** — attention mixes information _across_ token
  positions; the FFN then transforms each token's own representation
  independently (no cross-token mixing here). It's also where most of a
  model's raw parameter count lives. Meta-characteristic worth stating:
  there's real interpretability research locating factual/world knowledge
  specifically in FFN layers — Geva et al. (2020/2021, "Transformer
  Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories") show FFN layers behave like
  key-value lookups, and Meng et al. (2022, the "ROME" model-editing paper)
  found specific facts (e.g., "Paris is the capital of France") can often be
  located and edited by changing specific mid-layer FFN weights. Caveat to
  say out loud: this doesn't mean FFN does it all in isolation — attention
  still does essential work retrieving and routing that knowledge into
  context. Verify citation details before presenting.
- **Final Norm** — one more normalization pass before the output projection,
  so the final linear layer sees a consistently-scaled input regardless of
  how many blocks came before.
- **Linear → Softmax** — projects the final hidden state into one score per
  vocabulary token (logits), then converts those scores into a valid
  probability distribution to sample the next token from.

Nothing has dethroned this general shape as the dominant architecture since
2017, but there are real contenders:

- **Mamba** — a state-space model, linear-time sequence processing instead of
  attention's quadratic cost.
- **RWKV** — RNN-style recurrence redesigned to train efficiently on GPUs. Both
  claim long-context efficiency wins; neither has displaced attention at the
  frontier as of this writing — verify current status before presenting, this
  space moves fast. Within "transformer" there's still real variation worth
  mentioning: MoE (mixture-of-experts) routing, different normalization schemes,
  attention variants (sliding window, grouped-query, etc.).
:::

<!-- STAGE 1/3 (nexttoken-stage-1-zeroshot): zero-shot -- animated prompt->LLM->completion loop, 5 words -->
## It's ALL Next-Token Prediction {#nexttoken-stage-1-zeroshot auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual diagram-panel">
    {{< include images/nexttoken-zeroshot.svg >}}
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Simple prompting</strong>: no reasoning, no tools — the model just answers, one predicted token at a time</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="diagram-footnotes">
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Every token gets appended</strong> to the prompt, and the whole thing runs through the transformer again to produce the next one</li>
    <li><strong>KV-caching</strong> means you only reprocess the newest token, not the entire prompt — but the cache can expire, and when it does, everything runs through from scratch again</li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Every "answer" is the same mechanism repeated: predict one token, append it
to the context, predict the next one, repeat. The left pane is the raw
context the model actually processes; the right pane is what a real chat UI
shows you — notice the system prompt never appears there. The second
question in this demo is the key beat: watch the *entire* box (including the
first answer) glow and pulse through the model again, not just the new
question. This is the throughline for the rest of the section — reasoning
and agentic tool use are both just this same loop with more stuff stuffed
into the context before the next prediction.
:::

## It's ALL Next-Token Prediction {#nexttoken-stage-2-cot auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual diagram-panel">
    {{< include images/nexttoken-cot.svg >}}
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>Simple prompting: no reasoning, no tools — the model just answers, one predicted token at a time</li>
      <li><strong>Reasoning</strong> (chain-of-thought): "thinking" tokens generated before the final answer</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="diagram-footnotes">
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Every token gets appended</strong> to the prompt, and the whole thing runs through the transformer again to produce the next one</li>
    <li><strong>KV-caching</strong> means you only reprocess the newest token, not the entire prompt — but the cache can expire, and when it does, everything runs through from scratch again</li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Reminder for delivery (2026)**: don't let this diagram imply that tags
mixed into one freetext stream is literally how current models respond.
Newest-generation Claude returns thinking and text as separate,
first-class content blocks in the API response — a distinct channel, not
an XML tag interleaved into a single string of freetext. The
inline-tag-in-text illustration here is a simplification of the
*mechanism* (token-by-token generation, one block at a time) for teaching
purposes, not a claim about the real wire format.

Same question as the previous stage, same final answer — the point isn't
that reasoning changes the answer here, it's that reasoning is the *same
mechanism*: tokens generated one at a time, just wrapped in a tag and
usually hidden from you.

`<reasoning>` and `<user summary>` here are **illustrative, not a real
tag from any lab** — say that explicitly if asked. We don't actually know
ChatGPT's internal format; OpenAI deliberately hides raw reasoning
entirely, in both the ChatGPT UI and the API. What you actually see
flashing in ChatGPT while it works is a *separately generated summary* of
the reasoning, not the reasoning itself — a distinct generation pass
whose job is showing you a live-updating gloss, not a transcript. That's
exactly the distinction the two tag types dramatize here: `<reasoning>`
= the real internal deliberation (never shown to the user), `<user
summary>` = the model generating a *different*, shorter piece of text
whose whole purpose is to be shown. Both are still just next-token
prediction — that's the point — they're just aimed at different
audiences.

DeepSeek R1 is the one lab that's a genuine documented exception: its raw
output literally contains `<think>...</think>` tags, publicly confirmed
in the R1 paper. Worth mentioning by name if asked which lab (if any)
actually does this. Anthropic's extended thinking returns structured API
content blocks (`type: "thinking"`) rather than an inline tag; Google's
Gemini thinking models show a "Thoughts" summary similar in spirit to
ChatGPT's. "Ask it to think step by step" describes *prompted* CoT (the
2022-era technique); by 2026 frontier models increasingly reason natively
via RL training, not because anyone asked — worth saying out loud if the
audience seems to expect the older framing.
:::

     tool call token-by-token (same mechanism as every other stage), a dot
     routes it to a second box (Agent Harness) instead of back to the LLM,
     the harness injects a tool result as one complete block (not
     LLM-generated, so no token-by-token reveal), then the whole context
     -- including that result -- resends to the LLM for the final answer -->
## It's ALL Next-Token Prediction {#nexttoken-stage-3-agent auto-animate="true" .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual diagram-panel">
    {{< include images/nexttoken-agent.svg >}}
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <ul>
      <li>Simple prompting: no reasoning, no tools — the model just answers, one predicted token at a time</li>
      <li>Reasoning (chain-of-thought): "thinking" tokens generated before the final answer</li>
      <li><strong>Agent + harness</strong>: give it tools, a loop, and a stopping rule — it acts</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="diagram-footnotes">
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Every token gets appended</strong> to the prompt, and the whole thing runs through the transformer again to produce the next one</li>
    <li><strong>KV-caching</strong> means you only reprocess the newest token, not the entire prompt — but the cache can expire, and when it does, everything runs through from scratch again</li>
  </ul>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Reminder for delivery (2026)**: same caveat as the reasoning stage —
don't present the inline `<function_calls>`/`<tool_result>` tags as
literally how current models communicate tool use. Newest-generation
Claude returns tool calls and text as separate first-class content
blocks in the API response (a `tool_use` block alongside a `text`
block), not tags mixed into one freetext string. This illustration is
teaching the *mechanism* (predict, execute, inject result, resend), not
the real wire format.

**Harness** = everything wrapped _around_ the model — prompts, tools,
memory, orchestration code, stopping rules. The model isn't getting smarter
here; the scaffolding around it is getting better engineered.

The `<function_calls name="bash">` tag is made up for this demo, not
borrowed from a real system — say that if asked. There's no single
universal standard the way DeepSeek R1's `<think>` is real: native
tool-calling APIs (Claude, GPT-4+) return structured JSON, not inline
text tags at all; where inline XML-ish tags do appear it varies by
implementation (Claude's own documented tool-use format is
`<function_calls><invoke name="..."><parameter name="...">`, more nested
than what's shown here for simplicity).

The key mechanism this stage is built to get right: the tool *result*
(`<tool_result>`) is injected by the harness as one complete block, not
generated by the LLM word-by-word -- it's real data from actually running
code, not a prediction. Then the *entire* context, result included,
resends to the model for the final turn, same "whole box flows through
again" pattern as every other stage.
:::

::: {.notes}
No definitions box anymore — say entropy and entropy floor out loud instead
of reading them off the slide: entropy is how many different, equally
reasonable next words/steps there are; the floor is what's left even with a
perfect model, because the task allows more than one right answer. The two
softmax cards are the concrete anchor for that, so land the idea through the
example rather than a stated definition.

Softmax row (low/high entropy): this is literally the softmax layer from the
transformer diagram a few slides back, made concrete. "The capital of France
is ___" puts ~97% of the mass on "Paris." "My favorite color is ___" spreads
mass thin across dozens of completions. Same architecture, same softmax,
wildly different genuine uncertainty — because the *task* constrains the
answer differently, not because the model is more or less capable.

Entropy ladder: same idea, scaled from a single token to an entire product.
Token-level completion is nearly deterministic. By the time you're at "build
me a to-do app," there are enormous numbers of equally defensible answers,
even for a perfect model — React or not, which auth, what feature set. The
fan icons are a literal count-of-branches metaphor. Key point: this isn't a
capability gap, the prompt genuinely underdetermines the answer.

"How Do You Lower The Floor?" — two mechanisms, deliberately parallel cards
so the contrast reads visually: one acts at prompt time, the other was baked
in at training time.

Context lever: requirements, specs, and unit tests narrow the space --
"rarely to zero" is worth pausing on if pushed. A test suite defines a
pass/fail boundary, not a single implementation: different code can pass the
same tests, different prose can satisfy the same requirements doc. And on
top of that, in real projects you frequently don't know what you don't know
-- you can't write a test for a requirement you haven't discovered yet.

World Knowledge lever: this is the payoff of the physics-derivation
conversation from the "What Is Astounding About LLMs?" slide, one level
more general. The mesh is deliberately NOT drawn as separable labeled
layers -- that would misrepresent how these networks actually store
concepts (see: superposition, e.g. Anthropic's "Toy Models of
Superposition" -- features share the same weights in overlapping
combinations, not one clean subspace per topic). That's why the blobs
overlap rather than tile: physics, biology, grammar, history, and code all
live entangled in the same numbers, and you can't cleanly pull "the physics
part" back out even in principle. The caption is deliberately narrow in
scope: this only helps when the task has one right answer AND that
knowledge is in there -- for genuinely open or ambiguous questions (edge-of-
research stuff), this lever doesn't apply and the floor stays wherever the
task's real ambiguity puts it.

TODO (planning note, not for delivery): the old closing block from this
slide -- "a perfect model doesn't get you out of this," the "you don't know
what you don't know" bullet, and the blue "software that keeps evolving will
probably always need someone to specify it, guide it, and verify it." thesis
-- was cut from here on purpose, not lost. It's a strong, fully-formed
closing beat that belongs on its own slide (the human-in-the-loop /
specify-guide-verify payoff, tied to the job-security throughline), not
bolted onto this one. Build that slide before finalizing the talk; don't
let this thesis quietly disappear from the deck.
:::

## What Is Astounding About LLMs? {.smaller .scrollable .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="section-label section-label--lg">Nobody Was Surprised</div>
```

::: {.table-panel .table-panel--tight}
| Idea                                          | Date | Basis                                                       | Citation |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| **"You shall know a word by the company it keeps"** | 1957 | Distributional semantics | Firth, 1957 |
| **Language is highly predictable from context**     | 1951 | Information theory | Shannon, 1951 |
| **Words → numbers, meaning encoded geometrically**   | 2003 | First learned word embeddings | Bengio et al., 2003 |
| **World knowledge lives in the weights**             | 1997 | RNN/LSTM predates Transformers by two decades | Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997 |
:::

```{=html}
<div class="section-label section-label--lg">What Actually Surprised People</div>
```

::: {.table-panel .table-panel--tight}
| Milestone                   | Date    | Surprise                                                                                                                                                    | Citation |
| --------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| AlexNet                     | 2012    | **Deep nets crush hand-crafted vision features** — the starting gun for the whole modern deep-learning wave                                                   | Krizhevsky et al., 2012 |
| Word2Vec                    | 2013    | **"You can do math with meaning"** (king − man + woman ≈ queen) — genuinely unanticipated linear structure                                                    | Mikolov et al., 2013 |
| Attention Is All You Need   | 2017    | **Recurrence isn't necessary at all** — attention alone works, and it parallelizes                                                                            | Vaswani et al., 2017 |
| GPT-2                       | 2019    | **Zero-shot <span class="crux-word">multitask</span> competence** — violated the field's _own_, just-established fine-tuning assumption                       | Radford et al., 2019 |
| GPT-3                       | 2020    | **Few-shot <span class="crux-word">in-context</span> learning** from a handful of examples, zero weight updates — nothing in the training objective predicted this | Brown et al., 2020 |
| Chain-of-Thought Prompting  | 2022    | **Step-by-step <span class="crux-word">reasoning</span> just appears** — an emergent capability that only shows up at scale, never explicitly trained for | Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022 |
| ReAct / Tool-Using Agents   | 2022–23 | **<span class="crux-word">Agentic</span> tool use emerges from prompting alone** — the same next-token predictor plans, calls tools, and self-corrects, no new architecture required | Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023 |
| FunSearch                   | 2023    | **An LLM inside a <span class="crux-word">search loop</span> found new math** — not solving a known benchmark, a previously-unknown improvement to the cap set problem | Romera-Paredes et al., 2023, _Nature_ |
| Scaling Laws → GPT-3/4      | 2020–23 | **That these models <span class="crux-word">work just so well</span>** — dozens of dependent steps (e.g., a graduate physics derivation) that should compound to failure, but the weights had already learned how they're correlated | — |
:::

```{=html}
<div class="section-label section-label--lg">What Is Still Under Debate</div>
```

::: {.table-panel .table-panel--tight}
| Question                    | Debate                                                                                                                                                    | Citation |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| Chomsky's Universal Grammar | Contested — **evidence against innate grammar**, or just engineering that says nothing about linguistics? | Chomsky, 1965 |
| Reasoning, or just generalizing? | Chain-of-thought **looks like reasoning**, but the Reversal Curse shows failures a real reasoner never would — something stranger than either label | Berglund et al., 2023 |
| Form, or meaning? | Bender & Koller's octopus: a system trained only on **form**, never the world, could talk convincingly without meaning anything by it | Bender & Koller, 2020 |
| World model, or surface stats? | Othello-GPT found a genuine internal board-state model from move sequences alone — real evidence, but still just a toy domain | Li et al., 2022 |
:::

::: {.notes}
Full detail per row, for questions:

- **AlexNet**: vision, not language, but the shockwave hit everything.
- **Word2Vec** (Mikolov et al.): "anomaly that contributed to a paradigm shift"
  — see the embeddings-illustration caveat from the earlier slide.
- **Attention** (Vaswani et al.): true significance was mostly retrospective —
  it wasn't obviously the big deal it turned out to be, at first.
- **GPT-2** ("Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners"): arguably a
  paradigm shift on its own.
- **Scaling laws → GPT-3/4** (new row): this is a deliberately different axis
  from every other row here. The others are about a new *category* of
  behavior appearing (multitask, in-context, reasoning, agentic, search-loop).
  This one is about *density and precision* -- given a long, specific,
  multi-constraint prompt, how reliably does the model satisfy all the
  constraints at once, correctly? Kaplan's curves (2020) predicted the loss
  number would keep falling smoothly, and that prediction held -- but nobody
  had a theory connecting "lower cross-entropy" to "will nail a compound
  physics question with shown work." That translation was invisible until it
  had already happened; you don't know what a loss number means until you see
  what it turns into. Dated 2020-23 rather than a single year because the
  realization was retrospective and cumulative, not a single paper's result.
  Deliberately NOT the "emergent abilities" framing (Wei et al.) -- that's
  about whether capability curves are smooth or sharp, which is a separate,
  contested question (see Schaeffer et al., "Are Emergent Abilities of LLMs a
  Mirage?" if asked -- the counterargument that sharp jumps are partly a
  metric-choice artifact on top of smooth underlying progress). This row is
  making a narrower claim that doesn't depend on that dispute either way: even
  granting fully smooth, non-mysterious underlying progress, nobody could read
  that off a loss curve in advance.

  If asked "doesn't a long derivation have to get every step right, and
  wouldn't even 99%-per-step reliability compound to near-certain failure over
  dozens of steps?" -- yes, that math is real, and it's *why* raw single-pass
  next-token generation is not, in fact, fully reliable on hard multi-step
  problems (this is a real, open weakness -- see the reliability-gap findings
  on the "Progress, or a Plateau?" slide). The steps aren't independent coin
  flips, though: they're draws from one joint distribution the weights
  learned to concentrate on self-consistent, correct continuations (matching
  units, matching earlier substitutions, respecting the constraints implied
  by everything written so far) -- not the model getting lucky many times in
  a row. That's also the actual mechanism behind chain-of-thought and
  inference-time "thinking": externalizing steps so the model can check them
  against that learned consistency structure, rather than trusting a single
  hidden pass. None of this means it's solved -- it still fails a real
  fraction of the hardest multi-step problems -- but the fact that it works
  as often as it does, given how catastrophically compounding error *should*
  behave, is itself the unexplained part.

  Also worth being ready for: "wasn't it already known that factual world
  knowledge lives in the weights?" -- yes, and deliberately not the claim
  here (see the "World knowledge lives in the weights" row in the first
  table -- Petroni et al.'s 2019 LAMA probing of BERT, and GPT-3's
  closed-book QA results, both predate this and were read as confirmation,
  not shock). A single stored fact is an independent lookup. A 20-step
  derivation is 20 *dependent* decisions that all have to hold together --
  categorically harder than recall, and not the thing 2019-era "knowledge in
  the weights" findings were about.
- **GPT-3** ("Language Models are Few-Shot Learners"): paradigm shift.

New "What Is Still Under Debate" table -- these are open questions the talk
should flag but not resolve, distinct from the surprises table above (which
covers empirical events that already happened). Chomsky moved here from the
surprises table since "is this evidence against innateness" isn't itself a
surprising empirical result, it's an ongoing interpretive fight about one.

Also say this out loud somewhere in this section -- it's the old "Open
Question Underneath It All" slide, folded in here rather than kept as its
own slide: when an LLM solves a problem it's never seen -- grad-level
physics, olympiad math -- is it because it's close enough to its training
data that next-word prediction can *express* the regularity (language is
that predictable here), or because something is encoding actual
understanding/rationality in the weights, no longer just tracking language
statistics? Nobody has a clean answer -- this is a live argument between
(some) linguists and (some) computer scientists, not settled science. It's
the same underlying dispute as the reasoning-vs-generalizing row below,
restated one level more general: predict-vs-understand, rather than
reason-vs-generalize.

- **Reasoning vs. generalizing**: don't present this as resolved in either
  direction. The Reversal Curse is good concrete evidence that whatever's
  happening isn't clean symbolic/compositional reasoning (Fodor & Pylyshyn's
  1988 objection to connectionism generally, revived against LLMs by Gary
  Marcus specifically) -- but "very good generalizer" undersells it too, since
  the failures are oddly specific rather than a uniform degradation you'd
  expect from pure pattern-matching. "Something stranger than either" is the
  honest framing.
- **Form vs. meaning (the octopus)**: deliberately kept separate from the
  reasoning-vs-generalizing row even though they're adjacent. That row asks
  "what's the internal mechanism" (empirical/functional). This one asks "even
  granting a perfect mechanism, can a system with no sensorimotor contact with
  the world ever be *about* anything" (semantic/philosophical, symbol
  grounding). Different kind of claim, doesn't resolve by getting better
  benchmark scores.
- **World models vs. surface statistics**: included as the row where the two
  debates above actually get empirical traction -- Othello-GPT is real evidence
  of structure the model wasn't told to build, but it's a toy domain (a board
  game with ~60 legal-move vocabulary), and it's genuinely open whether that
  generalizes to messier real-world domains language actually describes.
  Framed as suggestive, not conclusive, on purpose.
:::

Engineering (harnesses, tools, retrieval) doesn't even get that far — no formal scaling law at all, just benchmark swings of 5–20 points from a design choice, not a curve over any resource.</p>

Open question: is this purely a **data-and-compute** problem? With infinite data
and compute, how good could these actually get?

- Counter-argument (Haikonen): architecture quality may depend on tacit
  organizational context — team history, roadmap, unwritten conventions —
  that no corpus, however large, could ever contain

::: {.notes}
TODO (planning note, not for delivery): pull on the "is it in the data at
all" string further before this talk is finalized. Haikonen's claim is that
architecture quality isn't a data-scarcity problem, it's a tacit-context
problem — the reasoning depends on things (team skill level, org history,
future roadmap) that structurally can't appear in any public corpus. I'm not
sure I buy the strong form of that: if good architectural reasoning were
genuinely captured *somewhere* at scale (proprietary codebases, ADRs, design
docs, code review threads) and just under-represented/hard to access rather
than fundamentally uncapturable, that's a data problem after all, not a
tacit-knowledge problem — "if it was in the data, it would be solved" is the
test to keep applying here. Go find out which one it actually is before
asserting either version on stage.

TODO (bigger, through-line for the whole talk, don't forget this): there are
two competing camps running under everything in this talk, and I want the
audience to walk away having explicitly noticed the tension between them,
not just seen it mentioned once. Camp A: if it's not in the training data,
models can't be good at it (data-encodes-the-ceiling). Camp B: reasoning/
rationality emerges strongly enough at scale that models don't need it in
the training data anymore (emergence-transcends-the-data). This exact
tension shows up in at least two places in this talk and I should make the
audience feel the connection between them explicitly: (1) here, on whether
good software architecture can be learned without architecture-quality
examples in the corpus; (2) back on the Knowledge Frontier slide, on whether
a genuine paradigm-shift-level scientific discovery (Einstein-level) could
ever come from a system trained only on existing human output, or whether
that requires something categorically different from more data. Same
question, two costumes. Build this as the connective thread across the talk
rather than two disconnected asides.

TODO (delivery idea, not yet written into the slide): work in the Hitchhiker's
Guide to the Galaxy bit on the inference-time card — Deep Thought spends 7.5
million years computing an answer and produces "42," a famously unhelpful
non-answer. Good comedic beat for the exact point this chart is making: more
thinking time is not a free lunch, and past some point you're paying a lot of
compute for very little extra coverage. Land it right after naming the
"best possible" band and before moving on to engineering.

The quote cloud and mechanism cloud below the four cards used to be their
own slide ("The Pretraining/Post-Training Dance"). Merged in and
deliberately de-tiered — the point isn't "rank these quotes by confidence,"
it's "look at everything labs have actually said, all at once." Two of the
quotes (o1, Opus 4.1) are the labs' own words; the rest are named insiders
or analysts, kept but not labeled as such anymore (solid border = higher
confidence, dashed = an analyst openly guessing, per the qc-solid/qc-dashed
classes, if asked to justify the distinction).

Important distinction if asked about Amodei ("scaling is probably going to
continue") or Altman ("there is no wall"): those quotes answer a different
question — whether pretraining is EVENTUALLY worth returning to — not
whether it has been happening FREQUENTLY recently. Not counter-evidence to
the quote cloud's claim; a separate, more speculative claim about the
future.

The mechanism cloud is the same disclosed-mechanism data the old timeline
used, itemized instead of dated or tallied: of everything labs have named
as "why this got better," pretraining scale shows up once (GPT-4.5) and
even that's contradicted by its own unchanged knowledge cutoff. Fine-tuning
has zero named entries deliberately — no lab has publicly credited a
specific fine-tuning technique the way they have for RL/reasoning,
architecture, or inference-time. That silence is itself part of the point.
Colors match the four cards above (pretraining/RLHF/inference-time); the
architecture/engineering items (multimodality, MoE, unified router) don't
have a card above, so they get their own violet, matching the original
5-icon lead-in before Engineering was cut.
:::

## Progress, or a Plateau? {.smaller .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<div class="diagram-split-row">
  <div class="diagram-split-visual" style="flex: 0 0 66%;">
    {{< include images/metr-time-horizon.svg >}}
  </div>
  <div class="diagram-split-text">
    <p>Two very different historical patterns to bet the future on:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Moore's Law</strong> — ~50 years of compounding gains, no wall yet</li>
      <li><strong>Compression / statistical sampling / symbolic AI</strong> — fast early gains, then a hard plateau</li>
    </ul>
    <p>Current evidence (from live tracking, as of this year):</p>
    <ul>
      <li>METR's task-completion time-horizon doubling accelerated to ~3.5 months in 2024&ndash;25, but is drifting back toward its historical <strong>~7-month</strong> doubling rate</li>
      <li>An inference-scaling study found only <strong>+7.1 points over plain chain-of-thought, and only at ~20x compute</strong> — a lot of "self-improvement" is buying small gains with a lot of compute, not finding something qualitatively new</li>
      <li>Real-world deployment (GDPval, enterprise benchmarks) shows a measured <strong>~37-point gap</strong> between lab benchmark scores and production performance</li>
    </ul>
    <p>No existing scaling law points to unbounded growth without either a real architectural breakthrough or an emergent phenomenon nobody's predicted yet.</p>
    <template class="slide-citations-source">
      <ul>
        <li>All 26 real data points (GPT-2 through Claude Mythos preview, Feb 2019&ndash;Apr 2026), across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google: METR Time Horizon 1.1 live dataset, extracted directly from the JSON embedded in <a href="https://metr.org/time-horizons/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">metr.org/time-horizons</a> (the same data powering METR's own interactive chart) rather than a hand-picked subset; methodology in <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks"</a> (arXiv:2503.14499) and the <a href="https://metr.org/blog/2026-1-29-time-horizon-1-1/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">"Time Horizon 1.1"</a> report</li>
        <li>Fitted trend line: my own least-squares regression (log2(minutes) vs. release date) across all 26 points, not a connect-the-dots line -- implied doubling time ~178 days, close to METR's own reported all-time figure (~188 days, per the same live dataset)</li>
        <li>"Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable": METR, same Time Horizon 1.1 report</li>
        <li>AI 2027's Agent-0 through Agent-4 milestones (definitions shown on the chart, each on its own line): <a href="https://ai-2027.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ai-2027.com</a> (Kokotajlo, Lifland, et al.) -- shown as reference points only, not connected by a trend line; exact task-horizon values for all five are not published as a data table, so their vertical placement is an approximate, illustrative reading of AI 2027's own published chart. Y-axis extended to 1 year to fit Agent-3/Agent-4; x-axis extended to 2030 to show where a possible data/compute wall might land</li>
        <li>The accelerating (violet) curve and the two faded background lines (slower growth, fits-and-starts) are illustrative only, not sourced to anyone -- not a forecast, just alternative shapes worth having an opinion about. All three share one anchor: today's date, at the point where it meets the fitted trend line</li>
        <li>Inference-scaling Pareto study cited in the 2607.07663 RSI survey (Wunderlich et al., ref 68)</li>
        <li>Enterprise agentic benchmark-vs-production gap analysis, 2026 (GDPval)</li>
      </ul>
    </template>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Master chart, deliberately dense -- combines several sources at different
confidence levels. All 26 real METR measurements are shown as dots (colored
by lab: grey OpenAI, teal Anthropic, blue Google), not connected point-to-
point -- METR's own chart shows dots plus a *separately fitted* trend line,
which is what the dashed teal line here actually is: my own least-squares
regression across all 26 points, not a connect-the-dots line. That fit's
implied doubling time (~178 days) lands close to METR's own reported
all-time figure (~188 days) as a sanity check.

A dashed vertical line marks today, at the exact point it crosses the fitted
trend line -- the accelerating curve and both faded alternatives share that
single anchor, rather than branching off different real data points (an
earlier version had them starting from o3 and Mythos separately, which was
inconsistent). Everything to the right of that line carries a very light
background tint labeled "Future," instead of a "Today" line in the legend --
the shading itself communicates that the region past today is speculative,
so the legend no longer needs a separate entry to say so. AI 2027's Agent-0
through Agent-4 are shown as amber reference points at their own scenario
dates only -- there is no drawn AI 2027 trend line connecting them anymore
(an earlier version connected today straight to Agent-2; removed per
feedback that the milestones read better as standalone markers than as an
implied trajectory). Agent-0 and Agent-1's dates (late 2025, early 2026) are
already in the past relative to today, so they're dimmed; Agent-2/3/4 are
still ahead. Definitions for all five are in a two-column box below the
chart, one line per agent (an earlier version paired them two-to-a-line,
which buried Agent-1 and Agent-3 mid-sentence). (Deliberately NOT labeled
with the individual forecasters' names -- Daniel Kokotajlo's/Eli Lifland's
separate "mode"/"median" trajectories from the original AI 2027 chart are
dropped.) Solid violet is a genuinely accelerating/super-exponential curve
(doubling time itself shrinking, not constant), same today-anchor. The
y-axis runs to 1 year (up from 2 weeks) to fit Agent-3/Agent-4's much higher
capability claims, and the x-axis now runs to 2030 (up from 2028) so the
illustrative curves reach out to where a possible data/compute wall might
land.

The two faded background lines (slower/logarithmic, fits-and-starts) share
that same today-anchor. Fits-and-starts is deliberately monotonic --
alternating rising segments and flat plateaus, never dipping down -- because
it represents the *frontier* (best available capability at each point in
time), which by construction never regresses, not an individual noisy model;
an earlier version used random noise that could dip, which was wrong. The
earlier "hard plateau" line is gone entirely: these models keep getting
better by some amount, a full flatline isn't a serious scenario worth
showing. This whole illustrative-alternatives concept replaces the old
separate "What Shape Is Progress?" slide, folded into this one chart instead
of standing alone. The legend itself was trimmed this pass -- dropped
"(real)" off the three lab entries, "(all 26 pts)" off the fitted-trend
entry, "(Agent-0..4)" and the "dimmed = already in the past" aside off the
AI 2027 entry (folded into "approx." instead), "(frontier only rises)" off
fits-and-starts, and the "small dots = other real models" line entirely --
all read as redundant once the chart itself already shows it.

The hatched zone and "measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable" caption are
METR's own stated methodology caveat, not my own commentary -- note Claude
Mythos preview's own real measurement already falls inside it.

Sources: METR Time Horizon 1.1 live dataset (Jan 2026); AI 2027 (ai-2027.com);
inference-scaling Pareto study cited in the 2607.07663 RSI survey (Wunderlich
et al., ref 68); enterprise agentic benchmark-vs-production gap analysis,
2026. All gathered/verified this research pass — see references/ folder.
:::

## AI and the Knowledge Frontier {.smaller .scrollable .heading-accent}

```{=html}
<ul class="frontier-intro-bullets">
  <li>Much of human knowledge is <strong>empirical</strong> — it needs a real-world experiment to verify. Some isn't: pure theory, checkable by reasoning alone.</li>
  <li><strong>Current AI progress is of the non-empirical type</strong> — nothing to build or run in a lab.</li>
  <li>Two modalities:
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Many attempts, verification in loop</strong></li>
      <li><strong>One-shot / few-shot, no verification in loop</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>The degree of sub-human, human, or superhuman ability is still contested.</li>
</ul>
```

```{=html}
<div class="frontier-split-row">

  <template id="chart-notes-template">
  <ul class="frontier-chart-notes">
    <li><strong>Scope</strong>: this chart only counts non-empirical results
    (checkable by reasoning alone) produced substantially by an LLM without a
    human directing each step. That rules out radiology, climate modeling,
    clean energy, protein folding, drug discovery, and diagnostics outright —
    those are empirical and/or heavily ML-pipeline-driven, not LLM-reasoning
    cases. It also ruled out materials science/superconductors on inspection:
    every 2026 example found (kagome-lattice superconductors, cuprate
    literature-extraction) is ML-screening-plus-DFT-plus-synthesis, not
    LLM-only theory. Economics/game theory: searched directly, found active
    tooling research but no flagship "AI solved an open problem" case —
    doesn't yet earn a dot.</li>
    <li><strong>Terence Tao rejects "superhuman"</strong> — "artificial general
    cleverness," not intelligence: ad hoc, often brute-force or stochastic,
    fallible, uninterpretable. On the Erdős problems specifically, "the true
    success rate is only a point or two [percent]... concentrated at the easy
    end." Verdict on an AI co-author: "on par with... a junior human
    co-author."</li>
    <li><strong>Color = number of public examples</strong> (green→red, log
    scale): Math/CS Lean-harness 97 (verified Lean-verified/checked count),
    Math/CS one-shot ≈90, Cybersecurity ≈6-7 disclosed across OpenAI,
    Anthropic, and Google (Meta excluded — not a true escape) — more than we'd
    originally counted, and plausibly an undercount of true incidents, so
    placed a little redder than the raw number alone would justify — Physics
    ≈3 (gluon-amplitude, cosmic-string radiation, a pre-1900-text-LLM
    rediscovery study), Computational Biology thinnest of all — GeneBench-Pro
    is a capability benchmark, not a list of discoveries, and no clean
    non-empirical biology example turned up.</li>
    <li><strong>Math/CS (Lean-harness) sits low on the y-axis</strong> because
    needing many attempts plus a verifier to land a correct answer implies
    weaker ability <em>per attempt</em> — even when the final, checked result
    is fully reliable.</li>
    <li><strong>Cybersecurity sits low too</strong> — every disclosed case is
    agentic, trying known intrusion patterns repeatedly, not reading source
    code and identifying the flaw directly.</li>
    <li><strong>Physics sits lowest of the "real" cases</strong> — beyond the
    one gluon-amplitude result, most 2026 AI-physics activity is either
    augmentation (tuning experiments, accelerating simulation) or rediscovery
```
